summary: This document specifies an updated format for Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers, replacing the one in RFC 4843. These are IPv6-looking identifiers derived from cryptographic hashes, meant for applications and APIs as endpoint identifiers rather than as network locators.

eli5.summary: A name tag made from a secret fingerprint can look like an ordinary address but still prove who you are. This RFC updates how those special address-shaped name tags are built.

questions: cryptographic hash identifiers as ipv6 addresses
what is the orchid ipv6 prefix
subtitle: A special IPv6-looking prefix for hash-based identifiers that name endpoints, not network locations.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as HIP want identifiers built from cryptographic hashes that existing IPv6 applications and APIs can use like addresses, without being mistaken for real IPv6 addresses. The first ORCHID format also had no way to change the hash function.
tldr.mechanism: An ORCHID is a 128-bit value: a constant 28-bit prefix, a 4-bit algorithm identifier, and 96 bits taken from the middle of a hash of a Context ID plus an input bitstring.
tldr.outcome: ORCHIDv2 replaces the format in RFC 4843 and gets its own prefix, 2001:20::/28. The 4-bit identifier gives each usage context a way to move to new hash functions later.

today: RFC 7343 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4843. It has been updated by RFC 9374.

sections.title: What an ORCHID Is For
sections.content:
Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers (ORCHIDs) are identifiers that look like IP addresses. They are meant to be globally unique in a statistical sense, non-routable at the IP layer and routable at some overlay layer. Each one is securely bound, through a secure hash function, to an input bitstring and a context tag. The input will typically, but not necessarily, include an encoded public key.

They are intended as endpoint identifiers at applications and APIs, not as locators in IP headers. The RFC names Host Identity Tags (HITs) in the Host Identity Protocol and Temporary Mobile Identifiers (TMIs) for Mobile IPv6 as expected users.
sections.eli5: An ORCHID is a name tag that is shaped like an address. It tells you who someone is, not where they live.

sections.title: Why a Separate Prefix
sections.content:
The point is to let people deploy protocol stack extensions such as secure overlay routing or HIP without rewriting applications. Existing applications and IPv6 APIs can carry an ORCHID as if it were an address. To stop an ORCHID being mistaken for a real address, and the reverse, the RFC asks for a separate prefix. That makes ORCHIDs compatible with IPv6 addresses at the upper layers and trivial to block at the IP layer.

The RFC says that using ORCHIDs between consenting hosts without coordinating with the IETF and IANA is technically possible but potentially dangerous. If the prefix were later used for something else, hosts using it would be unable to use it for the new purpose. It compares this to historical hijacking of IPv4 addresses that are not RFC 1918 private ones, and admits that using identifiers through existing APIs is arguably architecturally wrong.
sections.eli5: If everybody invents their own secret address range, someone will eventually collide with someone else. So the ORCHID range is officially reserved ahead of time.

sections.title: How an ORCHID Is Built
sections.content:
An ORCHID is made by the ORCHID Generation Algorithm (OGA), which takes an input bitstring and a Context Identifier. The steps are: the hash input is the Context ID concatenated with the input; the hash is the hash function applied to that; and the ORCHID is the prefix, then a 4-bit OGA ID, then Encode_96(Hash).

  • Context ID: a randomly generated 128-bit value that names the usage context and the hash function for it. It comes from the namespace of CGA Type Tags.
  • OGA ID: a 4-bit identifier of the hash function in use within that context.
  • Encode_96: extracts the middle 96 bits of the hash output.
  • Prefix: the constant 28-bit value 2001:20::/28.

The hash function must have preimage resistance and second-preimage resistance. Each usage document defines its own hash. As an example, HIP version 2 defines truncated SHA1 for OGA ID 3.

The result is 128 bits long. Because the prefix sits under the global unicast block, ORCHIDs are indistinguishable from global unicast addresses, although they do not follow the address format of RFC 4291 because they have no 64-bit Interface ID.
sections.eli5: Mix a person's unique fingerprint with a context label, run it through a scrambler, keep the middle part, and glue a fixed label and a small scrambler code in front. That is your ORCHID.

sections.title: Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
ORCHIDs are location-independent endpoint identifiers, so routers MAY be configured not to forward any packet with an ORCHID as source or destination. If the destination is an ORCHID and the source is a valid unicast source, routers MAY send an ICMP Destination Unreachable, Administratively Prohibited message.

ORCHIDs are not for IPv6 routing protocols. Any future overlay routing system based on them is out of scope. Router software MUST NOT include special handling code for ORCHIDs: non-routability is to be done by configuration, such as an Access Control List entry that blocks the prefix.
sections.eli5: Routers are allowed to throw ORCHID mail away. They do it because a network admin told them to, not because the router was built to know about ORCHIDs.

sections.title: Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
Two forces compete. As many bits as possible should be kept for the hash result, and the namespace should be shareable by several mechanisms. The design gives the maximum to the hash: everything after the prefix and the OGA ID is hash output. That leaves no room in the ORCHID for a context label.

The sharing need is met by putting the Context ID into the hash input. The mechanism cannot be read straight off an ORCHID, but one can check with high probability that a given input and ORCHID belong to a given context. The 4 bits of OGA ID give cryptographic agility for the hash function in each context.
sections.eli5: There is only so much room on the tag. The designers spent almost all of it on the fingerprint and hid the context label inside the fingerprint maths.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The binding between an ORCHID and its Context ID and input depends on the second-preimage resistance of the hash. A short prefix helps, because it leaves more bits for the hash output.

For a given Context ID, all mechanisms MUST use exactly the same method to generate an ORCHID from the input. Otherwise bidding-down attacks are possible: if several hash functions were valid for one Context ID and one became insecure, ORCHIDs made with the still-secure functions could be attacked too.

The OGA ID is in the ORCHID, and what its values mean is defined separately for each Context ID. Each application allocates a Context ID and its own OGA ID registry. This keeps the 4-bit space, which has 16 values, from being used up quickly. To keep collisions unlikely, each method MUST ensure inputs are unique or statistically unique within the context, for example with a global counter, a pseudorandom number with minimum 96 bits of entropy, or a randomly generated public key. Truncating the hash is similar to RFC 6920, whose security considerations also apply.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the same club must make their tags the same way, or a cheater could force the club to use the weakest scrambler. Different clubs can pick different scramblers.

sections.title: The IANA Allocation
sections.content:
Because ORCHIDv2 is not backward compatible, IANA has allocated a new 28-bit prefix out of the IPv6 Special Purpose Address Block 2001:0000::/23, as set out in RFC 6890. The prefix temporarily allocated to the experimental ORCHID was returned to IANA in March 2014. The registry entry is: address block 2001:20::/28, name ORCHIDv2, allocation date 2014-07, no termination date.

This document defines no specific Context ID value. Context IDs share the CGA Type Tag namespace, so new values follow RFC 3972, which is First Come, First Served, and no IANA action is required.
sections.eli5: The official address book now has one reserved page for ORCHIDs, and the older page was handed back.

fields.name: OGA ID
fields.desc: Identifies the hash function within the Context ID.

fields.name: Encode_96(Hash)
fields.desc: Middle 96 bits of the hash of Context ID followed by the input.
